region: West and Central Africa (Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Congo Basin)
description: Afrormosia is a fine, durable West and Central African hardwood that starts yellowish-brown and darkens to a teak-like brown. It is used as a teak substitute for furniture, joinery, flooring, veneers and boat work, and its trade is regulated under CITES.

hazards.summary: The UK safety regulator lists skin irritation among the reported effects of afrormosia.
The UK safety regulator notes that afrormosia splinters tend to become infected (go septic).
The UK safety regulator lists nervous system effects among the reported effects of afrormosia, without further detail.
IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long-term exposure.

known_compounds.name: 2,6-dimethoxy-1,4-benzoquinone
known_compounds.role: quinone isolated from afrormosia wood; a contact sensitizer in guinea pig tests

Heartwood a fresh yellowish-brown with olive and light brown streaks, beginning to warm toward a teak-like medium brown; a narrow band of pale cream sapwood along one edge. Straight to slightly interlocked grain with a subtle ribbon stripe, fine even texture finer than teak, small pores, and a smooth surface with moderate-to-high natural luster. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of afrormosia with yellowish-brown heartwood streaked with olive and light brown, and a fine even texture.
notes_internal: Only an agency listing (HSE-WIS30) found; no primary clinical reports on afrormosia found in PubMed searches ('afrormosia OR Pericopsis' with dermatitis/asthma/allergy/toxic) on 2026-11-07. HSE-WIS30 does not describe the 'nervous system effects'; route assigned as inhalation by assumption, flag for review. Botanical name verified on WFO: Pericopsis elata (Harms) Meeuwen accepted; Afrormosia elata Harms is a synonym. Hausen-1978 isolated 2,6-dimethoxybenzoquinone from afrormosia among ~21 woods; no afrormosia patient data in that abstract.
